title: A Look at Darkest Night 2nd Edition
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ChKL1KyjlZ4

Daniel (@dungeondive) covers Darkest Night 2nd Edition — a Patreon-voted pick — and makes a case for a game that looks mechanisms-forward on paper but has quietly won him over.

His framing is micro-elements. A hero takes one action per turn. Most checks are a single d6. Every being in the game, the Necromancer included, has one hit point. Flavour text runs to a sentence. Nothing is excessive, and yet the small parts compound into something genuinely evocative.

The theme is what he keeps returning to. The world is already lost when you sit down — as though you're playing after some previous group failed. Four heroes shelter behind the monastery's lighted border, the last safe ground, and they do not ride out declaring war. They move covertly. Each hero carries just two stats, grace and secrecy, both spent as currency: grace buys your way out of death, and secrecy erodes as you act boldly, until the Necromancer turns his attention on you. Daniel rates that trade-off as a concept he rarely sees elsewhere.

He also rates it among the best-looking games he's played — tarot-sized artifacts, muted palette, superb character art — and highly recommends it, if you can find a copy between printings.

----

Darkest Night starts you in a world that has already been lost, sneaking rather than charging — does beginning in defeat make a game more atmospheric, or just more grim?
